fields.title: Readiness
fields.intro: How the app decides each morning whether you are ready for the planned session.

fields.title: Training load
fields.intro: How much training you do, how it adds up, and how it compares with your plan.

fields.title: Cycling performance
fields.intro: Power, tests and how well you hold power over a long ride.

fields.title: Running performance
fields.intro: Pace and heart rate on your runs.

fields.title: Plan and log
fields.intro: Your schedule, your own log and reminders.

fields.title: Health log
fields.intro: A private log of what you take and your own records. Aevigor only stores and charts what you enter. It is not medical advice.

topics.title: Daily status
topics.short: One call each morning: Ready to train, Train with care, or Go easy today. It compares how you feel, your HRV trend and your sleep with your own normal.
topics.why: One clear answer saves you reading five charts before a session, and it is based on your own history, not population averages.
calc: The app checks four things in order. Feel from your check-in counts most. Then the 7-day HRV trend against your 60-day normal. A night under 6 hours of sleep lowers the call one step. Feeling sick overrides everything: below the neck means Go easy today, mild symptoms above the neck lower the call one step.

Ready to train needs Feel at or above your normal, 7 or more hours of sleep, HRV inside its band and no flags. Resting heart rate never sets the call on its own; it only confirms a low HRV and soft Feel.
Lifting does not change the status. The status only covers endurance training.

topics.title: Signals
topics.short: The numbers behind today's call, each next to your normal: Feel, 7-day HRV, sleep, resting heart rate and, when you have a plan, load vs plan.
topics.why: So you can see which signal moved the call, and decide for yourself.
calc: Green dot: inside your normal range. Amber: a little outside. Red: well outside. Grey: no reading today. Missing data never counts as a drop.
Your normal is learned from your own last 60 days (HRV and resting heart rate) and last 4 weeks (Feel).

topics.title: Feel score
topics.short: Your check-in answers (fatigue, soreness, sleep quality, stress, mood) turned into one score out of 25.
topics.why: How you feel predicts how training is going better than most watch numbers, so it carries the most weight.
calc: Each answer goes from 1 (best, 5 points) to 4 (worst, 1 point). The score is the average of the answers you gave, times 5. At least 3 answers are needed.

The score is compared with your average over the last 4 weeks. A little below your normal means Train with care. Well below your normal (more than one standard deviation, never less than 1.5 points), or any answer at the worst level, means Go easy today.

Joint pain (Achilles, below the kneecap, hamstring at the sit bone, knees, hips, elbows, shoulders, sole of the foot and more) is a plain log: you pick Joint pain on the body map and set Mild, Moderate or Severe. It goes into your intervals.icu comments but is not part of the Feel score or the status, gets no load number, and is not a diagnosis. Pain that lasts or gets worse is a reason to see a health professional.

topics.title: HRV 7-day trend
topics.short: Heart rate variability from your watch overnight, as a 7-day average compared with your 60-day normal.
topics.why: A single morning's HRV jumps around a lot. The weekly trend is much more reliable for spotting real change.
calc: The app takes the natural log of each night's HRV (ln HRV, so big and small numbers count fairly), averages the last 7 days, and compares it with the average and spread (standard deviation, SD) of the last 60 days.
Below the normal by more than 0.5 SD, or above it by more than 1 SD, means Train with care. Unusually high HRV can also be a sign of heavy fatigue, so it is flagged too.
On the Trends chart the shaded band is your normal range and the line is the 7-day average.

topics.title: Sleep
topics.short: Last night's sleep from your watch, with bands: 7 to 9 hours target, 6 to 7 borderline, under 6 short.
topics.why: Short sleep lowers performance and makes hard sessions feel harder.
calc: A night under 6 hours lowers the call one step. Two short nights in a row turn the weekly check to Watch.
The sleep bands match intervals.icu so both apps agree.

topics.title: Resting heart rate
topics.short: Your overnight resting heart rate as a 7-day average, compared with your 60-day normal.
topics.why: A raised resting heart rate supports other warning signs, but on its own it is a weaker marker, so it only confirms.
calc: High means the 7-day average is more than 0.5 SD above your 60-day normal.
Low HRV plus high resting heart rate plus a soft Feel score together set Go easy today.

topics.title: Sickness check
topics.short: The check-in asks if you feel sick. Below the neck (chest, fever, body aches) sets Go easy today. Mild symptoms above the neck lower the call one step.
topics.why: Hard exercise while ill, especially with fever or chest symptoms, is discouraged. This check only adjusts training; it is not a medical check.
calc: Yes (below the neck) = Go easy today. Mild (above the neck) = one step lower, and at least Train with care.
The above or below the neck rule is a common sports-medicine rule of thumb, not a tested cut-off. See a health professional if you are unwell.

topics.title: Weekly check
topics.short: Your week at a glance, shown from Monday and kept all week: where you are in the training block, key sessions, tests or a deload coming, appointments, and what to keep an eye on.
topics.why: Planning the week around the key sessions, and spotting a pattern in sleep, HRV or resting heart rate early, helps you train hard on the right days. Items already done drop off as the week goes on.
calc: Week of the block comes from the tests in your intervals.icu calendar, using the 5-week block: weeks 1 to 3 build, the VO2 test is in week 3, week 4 is the deload and the FTP test is in week 5. It only shows when the app can work it out.
Key sessions are this week's days with the most planned load in intervals.icu, plus any test or race. Appointments come from the Calendar tab.

What to monitor looks at the last 7 days: average sleep against 7 hours, the 7-day HRV trend and resting heart rate against your 60-day normal, Feel from the check-in, and load against plan. The deload check is the same as before: 7-day HRV below its band 3 or more days in a row = Deload; with resting heart rate also high = Deload, strong; 1 or 2 low days, resting heart rate high on its own, or two short nights in a row = Watch.
The advice is about training and recovery only (ease off, an earlier night, an easy day). It is not medical advice and does not diagnose anything.

topics.title: Trends
topics.short: Charts of Feel, HRV, sleep, resting heart rate, daily effort and load over time, each with a 7-day line and your normal range.
topics.why: Trends show slow changes that one day cannot.
calc: Shaded bands are your normal range from your own history: your 4-week Feel normal, your 60-day HRV and resting heart rate normal, and the 7 to 9 hour sleep target.
Drag the slider to change how many weeks are shown.

topics.title: Fitness, Fatigue and Form
topics.short: Fitness is your training over the last 6 weeks. Fatigue is the last week. Form is Fitness minus Fatigue: how fresh you are.
topics.why: It shows whether you are building, holding or tapering, and whether you will be fresh for a test or race.
calc: Each day's load is added to two rolling averages: a 42-day one (Fitness, also called CTL) and a 7-day one (Fatigue, ATL). Form (TSB) = yesterday's Fitness minus yesterday's Fatigue.
The numbers come from intervals.icu so both apps agree.

topics.title: Form zones
topics.short: Bands on the Form chart: below -30 high risk, -30 to -10 optimal training, -10 to +5 grey zone, +5 to about +20 fresh, above +20 transition.
topics.why: So you can see at a glance if you are training productively, too deep, or getting stale.
calc: For a test or race, aim for Form around +5 to +15 so you arrive fresh. A short taper improves performance.
The bands match intervals.icu.

topics.title: Ramp rate
topics.short: How much your Fitness rose over the last 7 days. Dropping below 0, Gentle 0 to 3, Ideal 3 to 7, Fast 7 to 8, Too fast over 8 a week.
topics.why: Building too fast for weeks on end is hard to absorb; building too slowly holds fitness back.
calc: Ramp rate = today's Fitness minus Fitness 7 days ago.

3 to 7 a week is a common coaching guide for building safely. Fast (7 to 8) is fine for a short overload block, such as a training camp, but not for weeks on end. It is a rule of thumb, not a research cut-off, so read it with your Feel, HRV and Training status.

topics.title: Training status
topics.short: One word for how your training is going: Detraining, Recovery, Peaking, Maintaining, Productive, Unproductive, Strained or Overreaching (plus Paused when sick, and No status until about 6 weeks of history).
topics.why: It puts load, performance and how your body is coping together, so you can tell good hard training from too much.
calc: Checked in this order. Paused: you logged being sick today or yesterday. Overreaching: high load and at least 1 performance drop and at least 2 signs of strain. Strained: 2 or more signs of strain. Unproductive: a performance drop while training is normal. Detraining: Fitness falling and 15% below its 90-day high. Peaking: Form +5 to +20 with Fitness near its high. Recovery: Fitness easing off. Productive: ramp 3 or more a week with no drops. Otherwise Maintaining.
High load: Form below -30, ramp over 8 a week, or more than 120% of this week's plan.

Performance drops (any one counts): EF below your 4-week normal on 2 rides in a row; decoupling over 5% on 2 rides when you are usually under; eFTP down 3% or more over 4 weeks; best 5-min power in the last 4 weeks 5% or more below the 8 weeks before (only if you rode hard lately); your latest FTP or VO2 test 3% or more below the one before; session RPE 2 or more above usual for the same intensity, twice; max heart rate in hard rides 8 or more bpm below usual; squat, bench or deadlift e1RM 5% or more down; or your last 2 sessions rated poor on your watch.
Signs of strain (3 of the last 4 days, against your own normal): Feel low, sleep under 7 h, soreness high, HRV 7-day below its band, resting HR above its band, or sick 2 or more days in 2 weeks.

Each check counts only when it has enough data. Missing data is never treated as a drop; with no performance data the app cannot call Overreaching. Uses all your sports. The cut-offs are starting values.

topics.title: Weekly load vs plan
topics.short: Bars of the load you did each week next to the load your plan asked for.
topics.why: The plan sets the load. The app only warns you when you do a lot more than planned.
calc: Load per session: power-based (TSS) for rides, pace-based for runs, and session RPE (effort 1 to 10 times minutes, divided by 10) for lifting, badminton and anything without power or pace.
Only sports that have planned workouts are compared, so like is compared with like. The alert shows when the last 7 days are more than 20% above plan.
The acute:chronic workload ratio is not used, because of known flaws.
This week by load type: TSS added up, next to intervals.icu's Strain Score (SS) and its three parts: SS CP, SS W′ and SS Pmax. Strain Score needs W′ and Pmax set in your intervals.icu Sport Settings.

topics.title: Next test
topics.short: A countdown to your next planned test, race or event, with your expected Form on the day.
topics.why: So you can ease off in time to arrive fresh.
calc: Tests are found by the name of the planned workout in your intervals.icu calendar: "FTP test", "VO2 test" (or "5 min test") and "Durability test".

topics.title: Power curve
topics.short: Your best average power for each duration, from 1 second to 3 hours. Medals mark your top three efforts.
topics.why: It shows your strengths (sprint, short climbs, long steady power) and whether they are improving.
calc: For each duration the app finds the highest average power you held for that long in any ride. Lines compare this season, the last year and all time.
W/kg divides power by your latest body weight from intervals.icu.

topics.title: Tests
topics.short: One card per test: VO2 (5-min max), FTP (20-min time trial), durability, efficiency (EF) and decoupling, plus 5 km and running efficiency for runs. Each shows your latest result next to your best of all time, the last 3 months or this month.
topics.why: Doing the same test the same way, every block, is the fairest way to track yourself.
calc: FTP = 95% of your 20-minute average power. It is good for tracking but may not match a lab threshold, so the app only compares you with yourself.
Tests are found by the name of the planned workout in your intervals.icu calendar: "FTP test", "VO2 test" (or "5 min test") and "Durability test". The ride with power on that day is used.

Durability = how far the 5-min max at the end of a Saturday ride of 1500 kJ or more sits below your fresh best 5-min of the 90 days before. Lower is better; about 5% or less is the target. Saturdays where the end effort was skipped (more than 25% down) are left out.

EF and decoupling use steady rides of 60 minutes or more (intensity 55-78%). EF = normalised power ÷ heart rate, higher is better. Decoupling = how far heart rate drifts up against power; under 5% is the usual guide (Friel). For runs, EF = speed in m/min ÷ heart rate on runs of 45 minutes or more.

topics.title: eFTP and 5-minute max power
topics.short: Your estimated FTP (eFTP) from intervals.icu over time, next to your best 5-minute power.
topics.why: eFTP updates from normal hard rides, so you can see progress between tests.
calc: eFTP is estimated by intervals.icu from your power curve. The 5-minute line is your best 5-minute power in each ride.

topics.title: Efficiency and decoupling
topics.short: Efficiency factor (EF) is power divided by heart rate on long steady rides. Decoupling is how much that drops from the first half of the ride to the second.
topics.why: A rising EF means more power for the same heartbeat. Low decoupling means good aerobic endurance.
calc: Rides of 60 minutes or more are shown. EF = normalized power ÷ average heart rate. Decoupling = the % drop in power per heartbeat from the first half to the second half. Both numbers come from intervals.icu.
Compare steady zone 2 rides with each other. Under 5% decoupling is a common target.
Heat, dehydration and fatigue raise heart rate at the same power, so a hot or tired day can look worse than it is.

topics.title: Time in zones
topics.short: How long you spent in each power, heart rate or pace zone over the last 4 weeks, 12 weeks or year, for any sport with zones.
topics.why: Most endurance plans aim for a lot of easy time and a little hard time. This shows whether your training actually matched that.
calc: intervals.icu works out each session's time in zones with the zones in your Sport Settings on that day. The app adds them up for the range you pick.
Power zones are a percentage of FTP, pace zones a percentage of threshold pace, heart rate zones are beats per minute. Your Profile shows the limits.

extra.text: Seiler S. What is best practice for training intensity and duration distribution in endurance athletes? Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2010.

topics.title: Lactate threshold
topics.short: Roughly the hardest effort you can hold steady for 30 to 60 minutes: threshold power (FTP) on the bike, threshold pace on foot, and the heart rate that goes with it.
topics.why: Training zones are set from it, and a rising threshold is one of the clearest signs your endurance is improving.
calc: Cycling: your FTP from Profile, intervals.icu's eFTP estimate, and each month's best 20-minute power × 0.95.
Running: your threshold pace from Profile and the critical speed from your pace curve, which sits close to threshold for most runners.
LT1 heart rate is your own number if you set one, otherwise the top of zone 2. Only a lab test measures blood lactate.

extra.text: Jones AM et al. The maximal metabolic steady state: redefining the gold standard. Physiol Rep. 2019.

topics.title: VO2max
topics.short: How much oxygen your body can use at full effort, in ml per kg per minute. Shown from your watch and as an estimate from your best efforts.
topics.why: It sets the ceiling for endurance performance and is linked with long-term health.
calc: Cycling estimate: 16.6 + 8.87 × your best 5-minute power per kg (Sitko 2021).
Running estimate: the VDOT from your best 5 km (or 3 or 10 km) time (Daniels and Gilbert).
The watch value comes from your wellness data in intervals.icu. All of these are estimates, not a lab test.

extra.text: Sitko S et al. Five-Minute Power-Based Test to Predict Maximal Oxygen Consumption in Road Cycling. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2022;17(1):9-15.

topics.title: Durability
topics.short: How much of your fresh 5-minute power you can still hold after a long ride. Tested as a 5-minute max after about 1500 kJ of zone 2 riding.
topics.why: Races are decided late, when you are tired. Durability is a separate part of fitness from your fresh numbers.
calc: Drop = (fresh 5-minute best minus tired 5-minute max) ÷ fresh 5-minute best, as a %. The target line is 5% or less.
The 1500 kJ marker and the 5% target are coaching choices for a non-pro rider.

topics.title: W′ battery
topics.short: Shows your energy above threshold (W′, "W prime") draining and refilling during a ride, in kJ and %.
topics.why: It shows how deep you went on each effort and how much you recovered between them.
calc: Above FTP (used as critical power) the battery drains by the watts above FTP each second. Below FTP it refills, faster when it is emptier and when you ride easier.
This is the differential W′ balance model of Skiba and colleagues. It uses your FTP and W′ from intervals.icu, so it is only as accurate as those numbers.

extra.text: Skiba PF, Fulford J, Clarke DC, Vanhatalo A, Jones AM. Intramuscular determinants of the ability to recover work capacity above critical power. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2015;115(4):703-713.
Skiba PF, Chidnok W, Vanhatalo A, Jones AM. Modeling the expenditure and reconstitution of work capacity above critical power. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2012;44(8):1526-1532.

topics.title: Work split
topics.short: A bar showing how much of the ride's total work (kJ) was done above FTP and how much below.
topics.why: Two rides with the same load can feel very different. This shows how hard the hard parts were.
calc: Total work = the sum of power each second ÷ 1000 (kJ). Work above FTP = the sum of the watts above FTP each second ÷ 1000.

topics.title: Sessions
topics.short: Your rides and runs with their key numbers. Tap one for its charts, or pick 2 to 4 to compare side by side.
topics.why: Comparing similar sessions shows progress better than looking at one ride.
calc: Numbers come from intervals.icu: load (TSS), average and normalized power, intensity (IF), variability (VI), heart rate, EF and decoupling. "Similar" picks up to 3 sessions of the same sport within 20% of the same length.

topics.title: Running performance
topics.short: Pace, threshold pace, and heart rate vs pace efficiency and decoupling on your runs.
topics.why: The same ideas as cycling, using pace instead of power.
calc: Run load is pace-based from intervals.icu, with heart rate as backup. Decoupling uses the same cardiovascular drift idea as cycling. See the Pace curve for your best efforts.

topics.title: Pace curve
topics.short: Your fastest time and pace for each distance, from 400 m to the marathon, over the last 84 days, the last year or all time.
topics.why: It shows where you are strong (short and fast, or long and steady) and whether your running is improving.
calc: intervals.icu finds the fastest stretch of each length in any run, so a 5 km best can be part of a longer run. Pace = time ÷ distance, shown per km. It is real pace, not adjusted for hills.

Critical speed is fitted by intervals.icu from your curve. It marks the fastest pace that is still steady for your body (the border between hard but sustainable and running out of steam). Most runners can hold it for roughly 20 to 40 minutes. It is only as good as your best efforts: if you have not run hard at several distances recently, it will read slow.

extra.text: Jones AM, Vanhatalo A. The 'Critical Power' Concept: Applications to Sports Performance with a Focus on Intermittent High-Intensity Exercise. Sports Med. 2017;47(Suppl 1):65-78.

topics.title: Strength numbers
topics.short: Estimated 1-rep max (e1RM) from your top sets, volume load (sets × reps × weight), and reps in reserve (RIR).
topics.why: e1RM tracks strength without testing a true max. Volume load tracks how much work you did for muscle growth.
calc: e1RM uses the Epley formula: weight × (1 + reps ÷ 30), from your best working set of 1 to 12 reps that day. A single counts as the weight itself. Warm-ups are left out.
Volume load = sets × reps × weight, added up per week (Monday to Sunday), warm-ups left out. Reps in reserve (RIR) is how many more reps you could have done; RPE 8 = 2 RIR.
Lifting counts toward load through session RPE in intervals.icu. It does not change the daily status.

topics.title: Muscle load (rides and runs)
topics.short: An estimate of how this week's training spreads over your muscles, shown as a % of your usual week (the 4 weeks before = 100%). Three views: rides and runs, lifting volume (hard sets against your volume landmarks), and all activities together.
topics.why: Lifting volume is counted in sets per muscle, but a ride or run has no sets. This card turns endurance load into the same kind of picture so you can see, for example, that a week of sprints and hills leans on your hamstrings and glutes more than a week of easy spinning. It is a general wellness view: it does not measure strain or damage and does not predict injury.
calc: Step 1, session load: the activity's Load (TSS) from intervals.icu. If there is none, session RPE × minutes ÷ 6 (an hour at RPE 6 ≈ 60, close to a steady hour's TSS). Activities with neither are left out.

Step 2, how hard: time in zones is split into 3 bands: Easy = zones 1-2, Hard = zones 3-4, Max = zone 5 and up. Power zones are used if the activity has them, else pace zones, else heart-rate zones. No zone data: the whole session counts as Easy.

Step 3, band weights: each band's time is weighted by how hard it is (Easy × 1, Hard × 2, Max × 3), then turned into a share of the session. Example: 50 min Easy and 10 min Max → 50 and 30 → Easy 62.5%, Max 37.5% of the load.

Step 4, muscle shares (estimates from lab studies, %). Cycling Easy: quads 40, glutes 20, hamstrings 12, calves 15, hip flexors 8, shins 5. Cycling Max: quads 25, glutes 22, hamstrings 22, calves 10, hip flexors 15, shins 6. Running Easy: quads 25, glutes 20, hamstrings 10, calves 35, hip flexors 10. Running Max: quads 15, glutes 20, hamstrings 25, calves 20, hip flexors 20. Hard = the average of Easy and Max.

Why those shares: in cycling, going from 150 W to an all-out sprint raised muscle activity about 7-9 times in the hip flexors, 5-7 times in the hamstrings and glutes, but only 2-3 times in the quads and calves (Dorel 2012), so sprints shift load to the back of the leg and hip. In running, the calves do most of the support work up to fast pace; near sprint speed the hip muscles (hip flexors, glutes, hamstrings) take over (Dorn 2012).
The figure has no hip-flexor area, so the hip-flexor share is shown on the quads (the rectus femoris is both a quad and a hip flexor). Running shins are counted in the calves area.

Step 5, running counts 1.5 × cycling at the same load, because landing makes muscles brake while they stretch. After 3 days of 2.5 h a day at 70% of VO2max, runners had about 133% more CK, 404% more myoglobin and 87% more soreness than cyclists (Nieman 2014); muscle-damage markers also rose after running but not cycling at the same intensity (Stocchero 2014). The 1.5 is our rounded, conservative choice, not a measured constant.

Step 6, muscle load = session load × (1.5 for runs, 1 for rides) × Σ over bands (band share × muscle share ÷ 100). Example: a 60 TSS easy ride gives the quads 60 × 0.48 = 28.8 (40 quads + 8 hip flexors).

Step 7, your usual week: the muscle's total over the 4 weeks before this week ÷ 4. The map shows this week ÷ usual week × 100%. Colours: well below (under 50%), below (50-89%), usual (90-110%), above (111-150%), well above (over 150%). A muscle with nothing in the 4 weeks before but load this week shows as well above.
Early in the week most muscles show below usual, because the week is not finished yet. Use the ‹ button to look at a full past week.

Lifting volume view: hard sets per muscle this week (sets at 0-4 reps in reserve; main muscles count 1 set, helping muscles half a set), coloured against your weekly volume landmarks MV, MEV, MAV and MRV (Settings › Weekly volume landmarks). All activities view: total load per muscle on one scale. Each lifting week's session load (intervals.icu Load, else session RPE × minutes ÷ 6) is split over the muscles by their share of that week's hard sets; sets logged with no session load count as 5 each (about an RPE 7 hour of 14 hard sets). This lifting load is added to the ride and run load, and the total is compared with the usual week in the same way.

Not included yet: hills and cadence. Uphill running loads the calves, Achilles and shin more and downhill running the front of the knee more, and a higher cadence lowered load on all three (Van Hooren 2024; Heiderscheit 2011). The app does not yet have the uphill/downhill split of each run, so hills are not counted.

Limits: these are averages from small lab studies, not you. Bike fit, terrain, shoes, technique and strength change the real shares. No validated per-muscle load formula for running or cycling has been published, so treat this as a picture of trends, not a number to train to. It does not detect or predict injury. Joint pain you log is a plain log with no load number. Not medical advice.

topics.title: Lifting log
topics.short: Log your sets (weight, reps, reps in reserve, warm-up) in the app, or import them from FitNotes, Strong, Hevy, Liftosaur or another app's CSV export.
topics.why: Your strength numbers sit next to your endurance training, so you can see both in one place.
calc: Weights are saved in kg and shown in kg or lb, whichever you pick. "Repeat" copies the sets from the last time you did that exercise.

Import reads the column names in the file (date, exercise, reps, weight, unit, RPE or RIR, warm-up) so most apps' exports work. Sets you already have (same day, exercise, set number, reps and weight) are skipped, so importing the same file twice is safe.

topics.title: Schedule
topics.short: Your planned workouts from intervals.icu, tests, and your own reminders, by day, week, month or the next 3 months.
topics.why: One place to see what is coming.
calc: Planned workouts come from your intervals.icu calendar. Reminders and repeating items come from My log.

topics.title: My log
topics.short: Quick-add entries for things you want to track, with repeat chips (every day, weekdays, every 2 weeks and so on) and reminder groups.
topics.why: So your own habits sit next to your training.
calc: Repeats use the standard calendar repeat rule (RRULE), the same one Google Calendar uses. Phone alerts can remind you at the set time.

topics.title: Phone alerts
topics.short: Notifications on your phone for reminders and post-session check-ins.
topics.why: So you don't need to open the app to remember.
calc: Turn them on in Settings. On an iPhone, first add Aevigor to your Home Screen (Share, then Add to Home Screen). Alerts are checked every 5 minutes.

topics.title: Medication and supplement log
topics.short: A private log of what you take: name, dose and time, with your own reminders.
topics.why: So your own entries can sit on a timeline next to your training. Aevigor does not interpret it.
calc: Aevigor only stores and shows what you enter. It does not give dose advice, missed-dose advice or interaction warnings, and it does not recommend products. Talk to a qualified health professional about medication and supplements.
The health log is a separate opt-in. You can delete all of it in Settings, Health log.

topics.title: Records
topics.short: Your own health records: blood pressure readings and lab or test results, with photos or PDFs if you add them.
topics.why: So your records are in one place you control.
calc: Lab flags (such as H or L) are copied exactly as printed on your report. Aevigor does not interpret results.
Charts show your entries over time with neutral colours only. This is not medical advice.

topics.title: Blood pressure
topics.short: A chart of the blood pressure readings you enter (top and bottom numbers, and pulse if you add it).
topics.why: So you can see your own readings over time and share them with your doctor.
calc: The chart shows exactly what you enter. Aevigor does not label readings as good or bad and does not diagnose. This is not medical advice.

topics.title: Labs and diagnostics
topics.short: A list of your lab and test results, with "One result over time" to chart a single marker.
topics.why: So you can find a past result quickly.
calc: Values, units, ranges and flags are shown as you entered them from your report. Aevigor does not interpret results. This is not medical advice.

topics.title: Last week
topics.short: How last week (Monday to Sunday) went: new bests, load against plan, sessions done, check-ins and Post Activity logs, and any test results.
topics.why: A quick look back shows whether the plan and what you actually did line up, so you can adjust the coming week.
calc: Load against plan adds up the training load of every sport for Monday to Sunday and compares it with the planned load in intervals.icu. Within 10% of plan shows green, within 20% gold.
Planned days done counts the days that had planned load and where you trained. Check-ins counts mornings with a check-in. Post Activity counts sessions of 15 minutes or more that you logged.
New bests are the achievements first set last week. Test results are planned FTP, VO2 or durability tests done last week.

topics.title: Achievements
topics.short: Your all-time bests: 5-minute, 20-minute and sprint power, best FTP and its gain over the last year, best running pace, longest rides and runs by distance and time, and your heaviest squat, bench and deadlift.
topics.why: Seeing bests and how they move keeps the long view in sight. A New badge marks anything set in the last 14 days.
calc: Power bests come from your intervals.icu all-time power curve (or your synced rides). FTP is the higher of intervals.icu eFTP and your FTP tests (95% of the 20-minute test), and the gain compares the latest value with the first one in the last 12 months.
Running pace is your fastest 5 km from your pace curve (or the longest standard distance you have run). Lifts are the heaviest weight actually lifted for at least 1 rep, not an estimate.

Firsts: a badge the first time you use each feature (check-in, Post Activity, manual activity, lifting log, import, reminders, phone alerts, supplement, medication or meal log, calendar item, health record, blood pressure, cycle log, connecting intervals.icu). Locked ones show a padlock.

Streaks count weeks in a row, Monday to Sunday. Weekly streak: at least one activity. Moderate compliance: the week's actual load is within ±30% of the planned load (70 to 130%). High compliance: within ±10% (90 to 110%). Weeks with nothing planned are skipped, and this week only counts once it reaches the mark, so an unfinished week never breaks a streak.

topics.title: Compare sessions
topics.short: Puts 2 to 4 sessions side by side: coloured bars for each metric, two power radars for rides with power, and both kinds of load.
topics.why: Seeing the same numbers drawn next to each other makes it quick to spot which session was longer, harder or more tiring.
calc: Bars: the longest bar is the highest of the sessions you picked. RPE is out of 10. Feel uses the intervals.icu words (Strong to Weak).
Power profile and PP · HIE · TP: see their own help topics.

Load: TSS is one number for the whole session. Strain Score (SS) from intervals.icu splits the strain into three parts: SS CP (steady work near threshold), SS W′ (hard efforts above threshold) and SS Pmax (short sprints).

extra.text: intervals.icu forum: Strain Score, a 3-dimensional load model.

topics.title: Power profile (Coggan)
topics.short: A spider chart of your best 5 s, 1 min, 5 min and threshold power per kilo, ranked on Coggan's table from Untrained to World class, with your rider type.
topics.why: It shows your strong and weak points at a glance, so you can train the weak ones or play to the strong ones (for example sprint finishes vs long climbs). Comparing a recent range with all-time shows which parts are improving.
calc: Each spoke is your W/kg for that duration, placed on the table: 8 categories (Untrained, Fair, Moderate, Good, Very good, Excellent, Exceptional, World class), each 5 of the table's 40 equal steps.
FT (functional threshold) = 95% of your best 20 min power, or intervals.icu's eFTP if there is no 20 min effort.
Weight is the weight saved on the ride in intervals.icu, else your Profile weight. Men's or women's table from your Profile.
Coggan has no 'climber' type. Climbing needs power per kilo at threshold, so it sits with time trialist.
The table's top and bottom rows come from the book; the app spreads the steps evenly between them as Coggan describes, so a value can differ slightly from the printed table.

Research mostly uses the Record Power Profile instead: your best power at many durations (about 1 s to 4 h) over a season. Coggan's 4-point chart is a coaching tool and was not tested in a study, but it is the only one with ranks for amateurs. Your Power curve card is the many-durations view.

extra.text: Allen H, Coggan AR, McGregor S. Training and Racing with a Power Meter, 3rd ed. VeloPress; 2019 (power profile chart). Summary by TrainingPeaks:
Coggan on how the table was built (40 equal steps between an untrained and a world-class anchor), quoted on BikeForums:
Leo P, Mateo-March M, Valenzuela PL, et al. The record power profile in professional female cyclists: normative values obtained from a large database. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2022.

topics.title: Morton 3P (PP · HIE · TP)
topics.short: A spider chart of Morton's 3-parameter power model, in Xert's words: Peak Power (PP = Pmax, 1 s), High Intensity Energy (HIE = W′) and Threshold Power (TP = critical power).
topics.why: Together they describe the power-duration curve with three numbers: how hard you can sprint, how much hard work you can do above threshold, and what you can hold for a long time. Each is trained differently, so seeing which moved tells you what your training is building.
calc: PP, Peak Power = Pmax, your 1-second peak power, from intervals.icu's power model (else your best 1 s).
HIE, High Intensity Energy = W′, the energy you can spend above critical power before you run out.
TP, Threshold Power = CP, critical power, from intervals.icu's power model. If intervals.icu sends no CP, eFTP is used and the card says so.

Morton's model: power you can hold for t seconds = CP + W′ ÷ (t + W′ ÷ (Pmax − CP)). The model check table compares this with your real bests at 5 s, 1 min, 5 min and 20 min; within about 5% is a good fit.
Each spoke is scaled to the highest value shown. The names PP, HIE and TP are Xert's; the numbers come from intervals.icu, not from Xert.

extra.text: Morton RH. A 3-parameter critical power model. Ergonomics. 1996;39(4):611-619.
Jones AM, Vanhatalo A. The 'critical power' concept: applications to sports performance with a focus on intermittent high-intensity exercise. Sports Med. 2017;47(Suppl 1):65-78.
Skiba PF, Chidnok W, Vanhatalo A, Jones AM. Modeling the expenditure and reconstitution of work capacity above critical power. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2012;44(8):1526-1532.
Xert: Fitness Signature (Peak Power, High Intensity Energy, Threshold Power).
